A repeated prompt is weaker than a constraint in the schema, extra properties make output less predictable, and removing descriptions removes guidance.

questions.question: After adding dozens of optional fields and several union types to a strict schema, requests fail with a 400 saying the schema is too complex to compile. Which response is BEST?
options: Retry the same request several times with exponential backoff between the attempts
Remove the schema and parse the prose that comes back with regular expressions
Raise the max_tokens value on the request so the grammar has more room to fit
Simplify it: fewer optional parameters, flatter nesting, strict mode only where needed
questions.explanation: Complexity limits are about the compiled grammar, so reduce optional parameters and unions, flatten nesting, and reserve strict mode for tools where violations matter. Retrying an unchanged invalid schema fails again, output caps are unrelated, and regex parsing of prose is the brittle approach schemas replace.

questions.question: A developer has corrected Claude Code three times on the same bug in one long session, and answers are getting worse. Which step is BEST?
options: Switch the project over to a different programming language for the fix
Clear the session and restart with a sharper prompt that includes what was learned
Keep correcting the same mistake, since the model will eventually learn from it
Paste the entire transcript of the session back in again as a new message
questions.explanation: Repeated failed corrections fill context with dead ends. A clean session with a better prompt almost always beats a long cluttered one. More corrections add to the clutter, pasting the transcript recreates it, and changing languages is unrelated.

questions.question: An engineer wants to understand how a large legacy module works before editing it. Reading it directly would flood the working session with file contents. Which approach is BEST?
options: Run the research in a separate, unrelated project directory on the same machine
Delegate the research to a subagent that returns a summary, sparing the main context
Read every file in the main session and compact the conversation afterwards
Skip the research entirely and make the edit based only on the file names
questions.explanation: Subagents explore in their own context window and return only a concise report, which protects the main session. Reading everything into the main context costs space and attention, guessing from names risks errors, and a separate project loses the repository context.

questions.question: A team installed fourteen Claude Code plugins. Sessions feel slower and token usage creeps up, yet most plugins are rarely invoked. What is the MOST appropriate action?
options: Disable unused plugins, because their skill descriptions occupy context on every turn
Ignore the problem, because plugins that are not being used cannot add any cost
Rename the plugins so that their skill descriptions end up a good deal shorter
Install additional plugins whose job is to compress the output of the other plugins
questions.explanation: An enabled plugin places the names and descriptions of its skills and agents in context on every turn, and its hooks and servers run alongside sessions, so unused ones carry a cost. Disabling or removing them is the fix. They are not free, and renaming does not remove the overhead.

questions.question: A team lead wants every contributor to a repository to have the same code-review plugin enabled by default. Which install scope is BEST?
options: Project scope, which records the plugin as enabled in the committed project settings
User scope on the lead's own machine, so it follows the lead into every project
No install scope at all; just email the teammates the manual installation steps
Local scope, so the plugin applies only to the lead and only in this repository
questions.explanation: Project scope writes the enabled plugin into the shared settings file that is committed, so contributors get the same setup (each still installs it on their own machine). User and local scopes affect only one person, and informal instructions drift.

questions.question: A developer is about to install a plugin from a marketplace that nobody on the team has reviewed. What is the BEST precaution?
options: Install it straight away and delete it again if anything looks odd afterwards
Install it at user scope, because that scope sandboxes it from the rest of the machine
Trust it, because every plugin marketplace is operated and reviewed by Anthropic itself
Review its hooks, commands and MCP servers first, because it runs with your privileges
questions.explanation: A plugin can run code, hooks and servers as you, whichever marketplace it comes from, so review the contents before installing. Scope does not sandbox anything, third-party marketplaces exist, and damage from a malicious plugin may happen before you notice anything.

questions.question: An agent fetches web pages with a client tool. Where should the application place the fetched page text when it replies to Claude?
options: Inside the tool_result block that answers that particular tool call
In the system prompt, so the model fully trusts the fetched content
In an assistant message that the application writes on the model's behalf
As a new user text block placed ahead of the tool result block
questions.explanation: Untrusted material returned by tools belongs in tool_result content, which keeps it separate from your instructions and keeps the required pairing with the tool_use block. System text is treated as trusted instructions, text before the result breaks the ordering rule, and assistant messages are for the model's own output.

questions.question: A team shares Claude Code settings that select the sonnet alias. After a new Sonnet release, behavior changes for everyone overnight. What is the BEST way to prevent surprise changes?
options: Switch to the opus alias instead, because that alias never moves to a new version
Disable automatic updates to the Claude Code application for the whole team
Keep the alias and ask everyone on the team to re-check their prompts every week
Pin the full model name in shared settings and migrate deliberately after running evals
questions.explanation: Aliases point at the recommended newest version and move over time, so shared configurations that want stability should pin an explicit model. Weekly manual checks are unreliable, application updates are not what changed, and every family alias moves.

questions.question: A developer wants sandbox URLs and personal test data available to Claude in one repository without committing them. Which approach is BEST?
options: Use a local instructions file at the project root and add it to the ignore list
Place them in the organization-managed policy file so they apply to every developer
Paste them into the very first prompt of every session by hand each time
Add them to the shared project CLAUDE.md so that every teammate benefits as well
questions.explanation: A local instructions file loads alongside the project CLAUDE.md for this repository only, and ignoring it keeps personal data out of source control. The shared file and managed policy expose the data to others, and retyping it every session is tedious and error-prone.

questions.question: An organization requires that no developer ever runs Claude Code with permission checks bypassed, even if individuals set it in their own settings. Where should the rule be placed?
options: In the project's local settings file kept next to the shared project settings
In every developer's own user settings file under their home directory
In managed settings, which take precedence over every other settings scope
In the shared project CLAUDE.md, written down as a clearly worded policy
questions.explanation: Managed settings sit at the top of the precedence order, above the command line, local, project and user settings, so individuals cannot override them. The other locations are overridable or are guidance rather than enforced configuration.

questions.question: A project's CLAUDE.md has grown to 900 lines and Claude Code seems to ignore some rules. What is the MOST effective improvement?
options: Trim it to concise, specific instructions and move situational guidance to skills
Add more rules so that each of the rules that are being missed is repeated again
Split it into twenty imported files, because imported files do not load at launch
Add bold and capital-letter emphasis to the important rules so they stand out more
questions.explanation: Long files consume context and reduce adherence, and contradictions make behavior unpredictable. Keep the file short and specific, and load situational guidance on demand. Imported files are still loaded at launch, so splitting does not help, and adding rules makes it longer.

questions.question: The authors of a plugin depend on another plugin, secrets-vault, with no version constraint. A new release of secrets-vault renamed a tool, and the dependent plugin broke for everyone who updated. What is the BEST fix?
options: Declare a version range such as ~2.1.0 on the dependency, widening it only after testing
Remove the dependency and ask each user to install that other plugin by hand
Tell all of the users never to update any plugin they have installed, at any time
Copy the dependency's code into the plugin permanently so that it can never change
questions.explanation: An unconstrained dependency moves to every new release. A tested range keeps users on compatible patches until the author deliberately widens it. Freezing all updates blocks fixes, copying code forks it, and manual installation reintroduces drift.

questions.question: An app has separate development, staging and production deployments. An engineer hard-codes one API key in a config file in the repository. What is the BEST correction?
options: Encode the key in base64 inside the config file so that it is no longer readable
Keep the key in the repository but make the repository private to the team
Share the production key with every environment so that all of them stay identical
Read keys from the environment or a secret manager, with a workspace per environment
questions.explanation: Keys belong outside source control, supplied per environment, with workspaces separating environments and their limits and spend. A private repository still leaks to everyone with access and to history, a shared production key widens the blast radius, and base64 is not encryption.
questions.whyTested: Configuration management for secrets and environments.

questions.question: Which TWO of the following are non-functional requirements for a Claude-powered support assistant? (Choose two.)
options: The assistant must summarize each ticket in three sentences
The assistant must call the refund tool for eligible orders
Model inference for EU customers must stay in an approved geography
Ninety-five percent of replies must begin streaming within three seconds
questions.explanation: Non-functional requirements describe qualities such as latency, throughput, availability, cost and data residency. Summarizing tickets and calling a refund tool describe what the system does, so they are functional.

questions.question: Which TWO workloads are good candidates for the Message Batches API? (Choose two.)
options: Answering a customer typing in a live chat window
Completing the next line of code as a developer types
Re-tagging an archive of 200,000 documents with a new taxonomy by next week
Scoring a 20,000-prompt evaluation set overnight
questions.explanation: Batches are cheaper and high-throughput but promise results only within 24 hours, so they fit latency-tolerant bulk work. Live chat and as-you-type completion have a person waiting and need synchronous calls.

questions.question: A team wants safe, repeatable changes to prompts and model versions. Which TWO practices support that? (Choose two.)
options: Store prompts in version control and release them through review
Switch the production model alias whenever a new release appears
Edit the live prompt directly during an incident without recording the change
Run an evaluation suite in CI and gate merges on its scores
questions.explanation: Versioned, reviewed prompts and automated evals make changes traceable, testable and reversible. Untracked live edits and automatic alias changes remove that safety and make regressions hard to trace.
questions.whyTested: Systems life cycle management for Claude applications.

questions.question: A client consumes a streamed Messages API response. Which THREE behaviors make it robust? (Choose three.)
options: Ignore ping events and keep reading
Parse every partial JSON fragment of a tool call as soon as it arrives
Read the final stop reason from the first event in the stream
Handle an error event that arrives after the HTTP 200
Skip event types it does not recognise instead of crashing
questions.explanation: Streams can contain ping events, mid-stream error events, and new event types added over time, so a robust client tolerates all three. The stop reason is null at the start and arrives in a later message_delta, and partial JSON is valid only after the block finishes.

questions.question: A reply arrives with stop_reason tool_use. Which TWO things must the next request contain? (Choose two.)
options: The tool_result blocks placed before any other content in the user message
A new anthropic-version value reserved for tool turns
An assistant message restating the tool output in the model's voice
A tool_result for every tool_use ID in the previous reply
questions.explanation: Each tool_use needs a matching result in a user message that follows the assistant turn, with the results first. Results are never sent as assistant text, and the version header does not change per turn.
questions.whyTested: Mechanics of the tool-use round trip.

questions.question: Which THREE are valid ways to supply an image to the Messages API on the direct Claude API? (Choose three.)
options: A path to a file on the application server
Raw bytes placed inside a text block
A file ID from the Files API
A URL that points to the image
A base64-encoded string with a media type
questions.explanation: Image blocks accept base64, URL and file sources. The API cannot read a path on your server, and image bytes in a text block are not interpreted as an image.

questions.question: Which TWO statements about the Message Batches API are accurate? (Choose two.)
options: Results are guaranteed within five minutes
Results can come back in a different order from the requests
It is charged at half the standard price
It supports streaming so results arrive token by token
questions.explanation: Batch usage costs 50 percent of standard prices and results are matched by custom_id because order is not guaranteed. Streaming is not supported, and processing can take up to 24 hours, although most batches finish within an hour.

questions.question: Which TWO errors are normally worth retrying with exponential backoff? (Choose two.)
options: A 429 response that includes a retry-after header
A 401 authentication_error for a revoked key
A 400 invalid_request_error caused by an unsupported parameter
A 529 overloaded_error response
questions.explanation: Overload and burst rate limits are transient and clear with time. A malformed request or a bad credential stays wrong until you change it, so retrying only adds noise.
questions.whyTested: Error type identification and recovery strategy selection.

questions.question: A bulk job keeps hitting 429 errors. Which THREE changes help? (Choose three.)
options: Raise max_tokens so each call does more
Bound the number of in-flight requests
Retry every failed call immediately with no delay
Honor the retry-after value before retrying
Ramp traffic up gradually instead of starting at full volume
questions.explanation: Limiting concurrency, waiting as instructed and avoiding sudden jumps respect token-bucket and acceleration limits. Instant retries worsen the burst, and max_tokens does not affect request counts.

questions.question: A team uses Claude Code to help with a large refactoring. Which TWO practices reduce risk? (Choose two.)
options: Keep refactoring commits separate from feature changes
Make small steps and keep the test suite green after each one
Skip human review because the changes were written by a model
Land the whole change as a single enormous pull request
questions.explanation: Small, tested, single-purpose steps are easier to review, bisect and revert. One giant change and skipped review remove those safeguards.

questions.question: Why do model-generated changes still need human code review even when all tests pass? (Choose two.)
options: Plausible but wrong logic and design problems can pass tests
Tests do not cover every behavior or security property
Model-generated code cannot be syntactically valid
The hosting platform refuses to merge any unreviewed pull request
questions.explanation: Green tests only prove the covered behavior, so review is where hidden coupling, security flaws and subtly wrong logic are caught. Generated code is usually valid syntax, and merge rules are a team policy rather than a platform fact.

questions.question: Which TWO are good practices when designing JSON Schemas for tool inputs and structured outputs? (Choose two.)
options: Make most parameters optional so the model has flexibility
Allow arbitrary extra properties to avoid validation failures
Write clear descriptions for fields whose meaning is not obvious
Use enums for fields with a closed set of valid values
questions.explanation: Enums constrain choices and descriptions tell the model what each field means. Many optional parameters and open-ended extra properties increase ambiguity and compile complexity.

questions.question: Which THREE habits keep an interactive Claude Code session effective? (Choose three.)
options: Delegating broad codebase research to a subagent
Restarting with a sharper prompt after repeated failed corrections
Keeping one session open forever so it learns everything
Pasting the full output of every command into the chat
Clearing the session between unrelated tasks
questions.explanation: Context is the scarce resource: reset it between tasks, avoid carrying dead ends, and keep exploration in separate contexts. A permanent session and pasting everything fill the window with irrelevant material.

questions.question: Which TWO statements about CLAUDE.md files are accurate? (Choose two.)
options: Block-level HTML comments in them are sent to the model with the rest of the text
They are loaded as context, not as enforced configuration
A project file always replaces the user-level file
Files found at different levels are concatenated into context rather than overriding each other
questions.explanation: All discovered files are combined, with instructions closer to the working directory read last, and Claude treats them as guidance, so use hooks or permission rules to enforce. HTML block comments are stripped before injection, and project files do not replace user files.

questions.question: A team will migrate from one Claude model to a newer one. Which TWO practices support a safe migration? (Choose two.)
options: Run your own eval suite on the candidate and compare results to the current model
Pin the exact model ID in production while the candidate is evaluated
Wait for the retirement date, then pick a replacement
Change the alias in production first and watch what breaks
questions.explanation: Pinning keeps production stable while you measure the candidate on your own tasks. Switching blindly or waiting until retirement removes the safety margin that the notice period provides.
questions.whyTested: Model version pinning and breaking changes across releases.

questions.question: The Messages API keeps the conversation on the server between requests, so a client only needs to send the newest user message.
questions.explanation: The API is stateless. The application must send the full history it wants the model to see with every request.

questions.question: A 429 caused by reaching a monthly spend cap will not be fixed by SDK automatic retries.
questions.explanation: That variant has no retry-after header and persists until the limit is raised or the next month begins. Retrying only repeats the failure.

questions.question: A refusal from the model's safety classifiers is returned as an HTTP 4xx error, so exception handling is enough to catch it.
questions.explanation: A refusal is a normal 200 response with stop_reason refusal. Code must check the stop reason, because no exception is raised.

questions.question: An error can arrive inside a streamed response even though the HTTP status was already 200.
questions.explanation: Once streaming starts, the status line has been sent. Failures such as overloaded_error are delivered as error events in the stream, so streaming code needs its own handling.

questions.question: Message Batches API requests cost half of standard prices, and results are matched to requests by custom_id because order is not guaranteed.
questions.explanation: Both statements are correct. Batch usage is charged at 50 percent of standard prices, and results can return in any order.

questions.question: Files you upload through the Files API can be downloaded again later with the download endpoint.
questions.explanation: Only files created by skills or the code execution tool are downloadable. Downloading a file you uploaded returns an error, so keep your own copy.

questions.question: On the direct Claude API, an image block can use a base64 source, a URL source or a file ID source.
questions.explanation: All three source types are supported. Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud currently accept only base64.

questions.question: Structured outputs guarantee that every value in the returned JSON is factually correct.
questions.explanation: They guarantee the shape (valid JSON that matches the schema), not the truth of the values. Semantic validation and verification are still your job.

questions.question: Assistant prefill remains supported on Claude 4.6 and later models.
questions.explanation: A prefilled final assistant message is rejected with a 400 error on those models. Use structured outputs or system prompt instructions instead.

questions.question: Server-sent events used for Claude streaming allow the browser and server to exchange messages in both directions over the same connection.
questions.explanation: SSE is one-way, server to client. A WebSocket is the bidirectional alternative, and the Claude API streams responses with SSE.

questions.question: The max_tokens parameter is a target length that the model tries to reach.
questions.explanation: It is only a ceiling. The model usually stops sooner, and if it reaches the cap the reply is cut off with stop_reason max_tokens.

questions.question: The official SDKs retry transient failures such as connection errors, 429 and 5xx responses twice by default.
questions.explanation: Automatic retries with short exponential backoff are on by default and can be changed with max_retries per client or per request.

questions.question: Using asynchronous code makes a single model request return faster.
questions.explanation: Async lets one process overlap many requests, which raises throughput. Each individual call still takes as long as the model needs.

questions.question: Prompts, tool schemas and configuration files belong in version control alongside the source code.
questions.explanation: They determine behavior as much as code does, so changes should be reviewed, traceable and reversible.

questions.question: A feature flag can switch traffic back to the previous prompt without redeploying the application.
questions.explanation: Flags are runtime switches, which is what makes gradual rollout and instant rollback possible.

questions.question: A dateless model ID from the Claude 4.6 generation onward, such as claude-sonnet-4-6, is a fixed snapshot rather than a pointer that quietly moves to newer releases.
questions.explanation: Anthropic does not change the weights behind an existing model ID; updated versions ship under new IDs. Convenience aliases that move exist for earlier models and in tools such as Claude Code.

questions.question: After a model's retirement date, requests that name it fail.
questions.explanation: Retired models are no longer available. Anthropic gives at least 60 days' notice for public models, which is the window to migrate.

questions.question: Updates to the system prompt used in claude.ai also change how the Claude API behaves.
questions.explanation: The consumer apps' system prompt is separate. Those updates do not apply to the API, which uses only the instructions you send.

questions.question: Claude Code loads CLAUDE.md files from the working directory and from every directory above it at launch, and combines them.
questions.explanation: Files up the directory tree are concatenated, ordered from the root down to the working directory. Subdirectory files load later, on demand.

questions.question: A plugin dependency declared without a version constraint follows each new release its marketplace publishes.
questions.explanation: That is why authors add a tested range such as ~2.1.0 when a new release could break the dependent plugin.

questions.question: Enabling a plugin at project scope automatically installs it on every teammate's machine with no further action.
questions.explanation: The committed settings record that the plugin should be enabled, but each collaborator still installs it on their own machine.

questions.question: A requirement that 95 percent of replies start within three seconds is a functional requirement.
questions.explanation: Latency targets describe how well the system performs, so they are non-functional requirements. Functional requirements describe what the system does.

questions.question: Usage of the Message Batches API reduces the rate limits available to the synchronous Messages API.
questions.explanation: Batches have their own limits, and using them does not affect Messages API rate limits.

questions.question: The token counting endpoint returns an exact count that will always equal the billed input tokens.
questions.explanation: The count is an estimate and can differ by a small amount from actual usage, so treat it as a planning tool and rely on the usage object for billing.

questions.question: Committing an API key to a private repository is an acceptable way to share it with a team.
questions.explanation: Keys in source control spread to everyone with access and live on in history. Use a secret manager or environment variables, with separate workspaces per environment.

questions.question: A support assistant must answer questions about a 40,000-row order database that changes every minute. The team pastes an export into the system prompt; it barely fits the context window and is minutes out of date. Which approach is BEST?
options: Raise max_tokens so that the model can hold the entire export in its working memory
Upload a fresh export through the Files API every minute and reference the newest file ID
Give the model a read-only lookup tool that queries the live database for the orders it needs
Send the export through the Message Batches API so that it is processed with each question
questions.explanation: For large, fast-changing data, let the model fetch only what it needs on demand through a tool: the answer is current, the prompt stays small, and access can be limited to read-only queries. A minute-by-minute upload still sends stale or oversized data into the context, max_tokens limits output rather than memory, and the batch endpoint is asynchronous and unsuited to live questions.
questions.whyTested: Messages API data access patterns: inline, by reference, on demand.

questions.question: A developer installs a plugin at user scope from the Claude Code terminal. Where will it also be available on the same computer without another installation?
options: In every cloud session run from a browser, because plugins follow the user account
In any teammate's terminal, because user scope shares plugins across the organization
Only in the terminal session where the command was run, until it is restarted
In the desktop app's local sessions and the VS Code extension, but not in cloud sessions
questions.explanation: The local surfaces read the same settings files, so a user-scope plugin is shared among the terminal, the desktop app's local sessions and the VS Code extension on that machine. A cloud session does not load the plugins in your local settings, user scope applies to one person rather than a team, and the install persists beyond a single terminal session.
questions.whyTested: How configuration applies across Claude Code interfaces.

questions.question: Because prompts are plain text, tuning a Claude application can safely be treated as a one-time design phase finished before the first release.
questions.explanation: Model behavior, inputs and models themselves change, so prompts need measured, repeated iteration: evals on each change, monitoring after release, and migrations when models are deprecated.

lessons.title: Choosing Between Workflows and Agents
lessons.summary: Who steers the process, code or the model: the decision criteria, the five workflow patterns, and how subagents and supervisor hierarchies split work.
lessons.reading:
Most Claude applications sit between two designs. In a workflow, your code decides the order of the steps and calls the model at each step for a piece of language work. In an agent, you give the model a goal and some tools, and the model decides what to do next, looks at the result, and decides again until it judges the task done. The difference is who holds the steering wheel: your code, so the path is the same every run, or the model, so the path depends on what it finds. Neither is better in general; the exam tests whether you choose the least autonomy that still solves the problem.

Ask four questions. Can you write the steps down in advance? Build a workflow. Must the same audited sequence run every time? Workflow again, because code can guarantee an order and a prompt cannot. Do you need predictable latency and cost? Workflows win, since an agent may take five turns or fifty. Is the problem open-ended, each next action depending on what the last tool returned? That is where an agent earns its extra cost and variance, and it needs guard rails: a turn cap, a spend budget and a clear definition of done. Start with one good call, add steps when measurements demand them, and add autonomy last.

Five workflow patterns cover most needs. Prompt chaining runs a fixed sequence of calls, each using the previous output, with code checking each intermediate result. Routing classifies the input first and sends it to a specialised prompt or a cheaper or stronger model. Parallelization runs calls at the same time, on independent slices of one job (sectioning) or on the same job several times to compare answers (voting), and merges the results. Orchestrator-workers lets a central call decide at run time how to split the job and hand pieces to workers, which fits work such as a change touching an unknown number of files. Evaluator-optimizer pairs a generator with a critic that checks drafts against explicit criteria until they pass or a round limit is reached. What separates parallelization from orchestrator-workers is who creates the pieces: you in advance, or the model on the fly.

When one agent is overloaded, with dozens of tools and a context full of tangents, split it. A subagent is a separate agent instance, started by a lead agent, that works on one focused task in its own fresh context window and returns only its final message. That gives context isolation, parallelism, tailored instructions and restricted tools, such as a reviewer that can read but not write. A manager or supervisor hierarchy is the result: a lead breaks the goal down, delegates and combines the reports. Every layer adds latency and tokens, so justify it with real differences in tools, permissions or context.

The most tested detail is that a subagent does not inherit the lead's conversation. If the lead spent ten turns learning that the public API must not change, the subagent knows none of it unless the task prompt says so. A good delegation names the files and functions, quotes the exact error, states the constraints and decisions so far, and says what the answer should look like. "Fix the bug we discussed" fails; "In services/billing/invoice.py total() raises on an empty cart; reproduce with test_empty; keep the public signature; report the diff and test output" works.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to agents? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: A workflow is a restaurant kitchen following a recipe card: the cook may be skilled, but the sequence of steps is fixed and every plate comes out the same way. An agent is a personal chef told "make dinner for six" who opens the fridge, decides what is possible, tastes as they go and changes plan. A head chef who sends an assistant to the pantry must write the shopping list, because the assistant was not in the earlier meeting. That list is the task prompt, and it is the only thing the assistant knows.
commonTraps: Choosing an agent because it sounds more advanced. If the steps are known and must repeat, a workflow is the better, cheaper and more testable answer.
Mixing up parallelization and orchestrator-workers: fixed slices you define in advance versus subtasks the model invents at run time.
Assuming a subagent can see the parent conversation. It receives only the task prompt you write, plus its own system prompt and project context.
Treating a prompt instruction as a guarantee of order. When a sequence must hold every time, put it in code.
Forgetting a stop condition on evaluator-optimizer loops and on agents: cap the rounds, turns and spend.
lessons.scenario: A retailer builds a returns assistant. Order lookup, eligibility checks and label creation always happen in that order, so the team implements them as a prompt chain with a validation gate before the label step. A separate "why was my order late?" feature involves unpredictable investigation across carrier notes and warehouse logs, so it runs as an agent with a turn cap and a read-only toolset. When the late-order agent grows to forty tools, the team splits it into specialist subagents for shipping, billing and inventory, each with a narrow tool list and a delegation prompt that carries the order number and what the customer said.
lessons.onTheJob: Resist designing the architecture before you have a baseline. A single call with good instructions often beats a clever pipeline, and a chain you can unit test beats an agent you can only watch. When you do use an agent, write the end condition and the budget first, log every tool call, and review transcripts: most agent failures are visible there as repeated searches, missing context in a handoff, or a tool whose description misled the model. Treat each added layer, whether a subagent, a supervisor or an evaluator, as something that must pay for its latency and tokens with a measurable gain.

lessons.title: Building Agents: Loops, Harnesses, Hooks and Hosting
lessons.summary: The tool-use loop, three ways to own the harness (custom loop, Agent SDK, Managed Agents), limits, permissions and hooks, plus memory, context and frameworks.
lessons.reading:
Under every agent is the same loop. You send the model a prompt and a list of tools. If it replies with a tool request (stop_reason tool_use on the Messages API), your code runs the tool, appends the outcome as a tool_result, and calls the model again. When a reply arrives with no tool request, the loop ends. The model never executes anything itself; it emits structured requests, and the software around it, the harness, runs the loop, enforces permissions, manages context and persists state.

There are three ways to own it. You can write it yourself on the Messages API: a loop that checks stop_reason, runs every requested tool, and sends back one user message holding a tool_result per tool_use ID, results first. That costs code but gives full control for approval gates and custom logging; the SDK tool runner automates the plain case. You can embed the Claude Agent SDK for Python or TypeScript, which brings Claude Code's loop, built-in tools such as Read, Edit and Bash, permissions, sessions, hooks and subagents into your own process. Or you can use Claude Managed Agents, where Anthropic hosts the harness: you define an agent (model, prompt, tools) and an environment, then start sessions that stream events and keep history server-side. The environment is either an Anthropic-managed cloud sandbox or a self-hosted sandbox, where tool execution, files and network egress stay on your infrastructure while orchestration stays on Anthropic's side. Managed Agents suits long-running, asynchronous work; because it is stateful, it is not currently eligible for zero data retention.

Control comes from code, not prose. Give every run turn and budget limits (max_turns and max_budget_usd in the Agent SDK). When one is hit, the final result message carries an error subtype such as error_max_turns and no result text, so check the subtype first and use the session ID to resume. Permission modes set how much approval tools need, from asking by default up to bypassPermissions, which belongs only in containers and CI. Hooks run your code at fixed points: a PreToolUse hook can deny a call before the tool runs, a PostToolUse hook can audit it, and neither costs context tokens. The principle behind all of it is programmatic enforcement: a rule in a prompt or CLAUDE.md makes the behavior likely, while a hook or permission rule makes it certain, so anything that must always hold belongs in code.

Long runs also need memory and context care. The window accumulates every prompt and tool result, so older turns get compacted into summaries and a rule stated only in the first message can be lost. Keep persistent rules in the system prompt or CLAUDE.md, push noisy investigation into subagents so only summaries return, and give the agent a persistent memory store for facts that must outlive a session. Frameworks package these ideas: LangGraph models a flow as a graph of deterministic and model-driven steps with durable state and human-in-the-loop pauses, PydanticAI offers typed tools and validated outputs, and Strands Agents is an open-source toolkit for production agents. They save work on state, tracing and orchestration but add abstraction, and underneath they still run the same tool-use contract. Start with the simplest loop that works.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to agent harnesses? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Picture a capable new employee (the model) and the office around them (the harness). The employee proposes actions: "I would like to email this customer." The office decides what happens: a checklist runs first (hooks), there is a spending limit (budget), large amounts need a manager's signature (approval), and the cash drawer is locked (permission rules). A memo reminding the employee to be careful (a prompt) helps, but it is the locked drawer that actually protects the money. You can run the office yourself, rent a managed one from Anthropic, or put the office on your own premises while the manager works remotely.
commonTraps: Treating a prompt or CLAUDE.md rule as enforcement. Only hooks, permission rules, validation in code and sandboxes hold every time.
Reading the result field without checking the result subtype. Only the success subtype carries result text.
Leaving a tool_use unanswered, or placing text before the tool_result blocks, which produces a 400 error. Answer every ID, results first.
Thinking a self-hosted sandbox keeps everything from Anthropic. Execution and files stay with you, but tool inputs and results still reach the model.
Adopting a heavy framework before a short loop or the SDK has proved insufficient.
lessons.scenario: A bank's platform team wants an agent that reconciles ledger exports overnight. The work takes hours and nobody waits for it, so they compare options. Building a loop gives control but means writing sandboxing and tool execution. The Agent SDK in their own service gives the Claude Code toolset but they must host it. Managed Agents with a self-hosted sandbox keeps the ledger files inside their network while Anthropic runs the loop. They choose that, add a spend budget and turn limit, deny any write outside the working directory with a PreToolUse rule, and require a person to approve any adjustment above a threshold.
lessons.onTheJob: Log every tool call with its arguments, result and the request ID of the model call that asked for it; those traces are how you debug an agent. Decide in advance what happens at each limit: a run that hits its turn cap should save its session ID and report partial progress, not crash. Keep hooks small and fast, because they run on every matching tool call. Test the failure paths on purpose, for example a tool that times out, a denied call and a refused request, since the happy path is rarely where an agent breaks.

lessons.title: Claude API Mechanics: Messages, Stop Reasons, Streaming and Files
lessons.summary: The request and response shape, stateless multi-turn conversations, every stop_reason, streaming events, structured outputs with defensive parsing, files and the Batches API.
lessons.reading:
A request to POST /v1/messages needs a model, a max_tokens cap and a messages array of turns tagged user or assistant, with standing instructions in the top-level system field. The API is stateless: the server remembers nothing, so your application resends the whole conversation, earlier assistant replies included, on every call, and decides how to trim or summarise it as it grows. A reply's content is an array of blocks such as text, tool_use and thinking, so loop over the blocks and check each type instead of assuming the first is text. Log the usage object, which holds the token counts, on every call.

Every successful response carries a stop_reason, and handling it is the heart of a robust client. end_turn means the model finished. max_tokens means it hit your cap, so the text may stop mid-sentence, mid-JSON or mid-tool-call: raise the cap, ask it to continue, or stream. stop_sequence means it emitted one of your stop strings. tool_use means it wants tools run, and every ID needs a tool_result. pause_turn means a server-side tool loop, such as web search, hit its iteration limit, so send the assistant content back unchanged. refusal means the safety classifiers declined; it is a normal 200 response, so no exception fires, and the content may be empty. model_context_window_exceeded means input plus output filled the window. Truncation and refusal are successful responses that need their own branches, not errors.

Set stream to true and the API sends server-sent events: message_start, then for each content block a content_block_start, a run of content_block_delta events and a content_block_stop, then message_delta, which carries the stop_reason and cumulative usage, and message_stop. An error event such as overloaded_error can arrive after the 200 status, so streaming code needs its own failure handling. Text arrives as text_delta; tool arguments arrive as input_json_delta fragments that are valid JSON only once the block stops, so accumulate, then parse. Streaming makes answers feel instant and suits very large max_tokens, since the SDKs reject non-streaming calls expected to run beyond about ten minutes.

When code consumes the output, do not rely on "please reply in JSON". Structured outputs (a JSON Schema in output_config.format) constrain decoding so the text parses and matches. Assistant prefill is rejected with a 400 error on Claude 4.6 and later. Constrained output guarantees shape, not truth, and a refusal or a reply cut off at max_tokens can still escape the schema, so parse defensively: check stop_reason, catch failures, validate business rules, and keep a retry or fallback.

Images and PDFs enter as image and document blocks from base64, a URL or a Files API file ID. Upload once and reuse the ID, but files are visible workspace-wide, so never accept file IDs from end users; Word and Excel files must first become text or PDF. For bulk work nobody waits on, the Message Batches API costs half the standard price, takes up to 100,000 requests or 256 MB, and returns results within 24 hours. Give each request a unique custom_id because results arrive in any order, dry-run the request shape on the Messages API because validation happens after submission, and handle all four outcomes: succeeded, errored, canceled and expired.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to the Messages API? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of a postal chess game where the other player has no memory. Each time you write, you must enclose the entire game so far, because they will read it fresh. Their reply always ends with a note on why they stopped: they finished, they ran out of paper (the output cap), they want you to look something up and report back (a tool request), or they declined to answer. Streaming is the other player reading their reply aloud as they write it. A batch is mailing a thousand games overnight at a discount and collecting the answers in the morning, in whatever order they finish.
commonTraps: Sending only the newest message and expecting the model to remember. The API is stateless, so the full history goes in every request.
Treating a max_tokens or refusal response as a failure to retry unchanged. Both are successful responses; truncation needs a higher cap or a continuation, a refusal needs a fallback.
Parsing partial_json fragments before the block stops, or reading the stop reason from the first streaming event, where it is null.
Believing structured outputs make values correct. They guarantee shape, so semantic validation is still required.
Pairing batch results with inputs by position instead of custom_id, or sending prefill to a 4.6-generation or later model.
lessons.scenario: A document-intelligence team extracts fields from supplier invoices. Interactive uploads stream to a review screen as they are processed, using the Messages API with a schema in structured outputs and a check on stop_reason before parsing. Truncated replies on very long invoices are retried with a higher cap and a streamed call. A nightly job re-extracts the archive: it is submitted as batches with the supplier ID as custom_id, one request of each shape having been tested synchronously first, and the results are joined back by ID. PDFs that are reused are uploaded once and referenced by file ID.
lessons.onTheJob: Wrap the SDK in one small module so retries, logging, model IDs and the stop_reason switch live in a single place. Log the usage object, the stop reason and the request ID for every call; those three fields explain most production mysteries. Write unit tests with canned responses for each stop reason, including an empty refusal and a truncated tool call, because those rarely appear in manual testing. Keep a dry-run script that sends one request of every shape through the Messages API before any big batch is submitted.

lessons.title: Application Design and Configuration Management
lessons.summary: How instructions differ across claude.ai, the API and Claude Code, content boundaries, schema design, session hygiene, plugins, and the configuration that keeps behavior stable.
lessons.reading:
Claude never works alone, because each interface wraps it in different instructions. The claude.ai site and the mobile apps add an Anthropic-written system prompt that supplies things like the current date and formatting habits. The raw API adds nothing, so everything you want must be in your own system prompt and messages. Claude Code adds its own instructions and loads your CLAUDE.md files, and the Agent SDK embeds that same loop in your code. The consequence is practical: a prompt that works beautifully in a chat window has to be rebuilt, and retested, inside your application.

Two design habits matter in every interface. The first is a content boundary: keep your trusted rules in the system prompt and place documents, web pages and tool output in clearly delimited, labelled blocks, with tool output inside tool_result, and say that the block is data. It is a design aid, not a guarantee, so pair it with least-privilege tools. The second is schema design. A schema is both a contract and documentation, so name fields clearly, describe the ones that are not obvious, use enums for closed sets, mark fields required where you can, keep nesting shallow, and set additionalProperties to false. Every optional parameter and union type adds ambiguity and, with strict schemas, compile complexity, so when the API says a schema is too complex, simplify it instead of retrying.

In Claude Code the scarce resource is context, so practice session hygiene. Clear the session between unrelated tasks. If you have corrected the same mistake two or three times, clear and restart with a sharper prompt that includes what you learned. Send broad research to a subagent so only a summary returns, compact with instructions when a long task must continue, and name sessions you will resume. Plugins package skills, subagents, hooks and MCP servers as one installable unit from a marketplace. Pick an install scope: user (you, every project), project (everyone, through the committed settings, although each teammate still installs it) or local (you, this repository). Every enabled plugin places its skill and agent descriptions in context on every turn, so disable the ones you do not use, and review a plugin before installing because it runs code with your privileges.

Configuration management keeps behavior stable. CLAUDE.md files at managed, user, project and local levels are concatenated rather than overridden, with instructions nearer the working directory read last. Keep them short, specific and free of contradictions, move situational guidance into path-scoped rules or skills, and remember they are guidance, not enforcement. Settings have a precedence order: managed settings, then the command line, then local project, shared project and user settings, with list-type keys such as permission allow rules merging across scopes. Put team defaults in the committed project file, personal overrides in the local file, and non-negotiable policy in managed settings. Finally, pin versions: use the full model ID rather than an alias that follows the newest release, version prompts in source control with an identifier you log, and declare a tested range such as ~2.1.0 on plugin dependencies so an upstream release cannot silently break you.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to application design? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Imagine hiring a translator through three agencies. One agency briefs the translator with its own house rules before every job (the chat apps). Another sends the translator to you with no briefing at all (the API), so you must supply every instruction. A third sends the translator with your company handbook already in their bag (Claude Code and CLAUDE.md). Documents you hand over for translation go in a labelled folder so no one mistakes a sentence inside them for an instruction from the boss. And you write in the contract which translator you want by name, not "whoever is newest this month".
commonTraps: Expecting API behavior to match claude.ai. The chat apps add their own system prompt; the API does not.
Believing CLAUDE.md or a boundary tag enforces anything. Both are guidance the model weighs; hooks and permission rules enforce.
Using an alias in shared production configuration. Aliases move to the newest release, so pin the full model ID and migrate after evals.
Assuming project-scope plugins appear on every teammate's machine automatically; each person still installs them, and every enabled plugin costs context.
Putting a personal preference in the shared project CLAUDE.md instead of the local file, or putting a mandatory policy anywhere but managed settings.
lessons.scenario: A platform team rolls out Claude Code to eighty engineers. The managed settings file forbids bypassing permissions and sets the allowed model list. The repository's CLAUDE.md is trimmed to 150 lines of build commands and conventions, with API rules moved to a path-scoped rules file and personal sandbox URLs left to each developer's local file. The shared settings pin the full model ID. A review plugin is enabled at project scope, with its dependency constrained to a tested range. Engineers are told to clear sessions between tasks and to hand research to subagents.
lessons.onTheJob: Audit instructions the way you audit code: run the context command to see what actually loaded, delete rules that nobody can verify, and resolve contradictions between nested files. Treat model and prompt changes as releases with a changelog and an eval run, and keep the previous pinned ID available for rollback. Review plugins before approving them for a team, check their context cost, and prefer a short list that people actually use. When behavior surprises you, ask first which interface and which instruction layers were involved.

lessons.title: Requirements, Life Cycle and Reliable Engineering
lessons.summary: Turning business needs into measurable requirements, choosing realtime or batch and a platform, handling errors and rate limits, and running the system through its life cycle.
lessons.reading:
Start with requirements. A functional requirement says what the system must do, such as extract an invoice total or call a refund tool. A non-functional requirement says how well: p95 latency, throughput, availability, cost per request, data residency, compliance. "Fast and accurate" is not a requirement until it becomes numbers you can test. These choices drive the architecture. A person watching a screen needs a streamed, synchronous call, while an overnight job belongs in a batch at half price. Residency may call for inference_geo set to us, or for a cloud platform such as Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud, Microsoft Foundry or Claude Platform on AWS, with their own IAM and billing but different features and limits. A zero-data-retention arrangement rules out the Files API, batches and Managed Agents for that data.

Capacity is part of the requirement. Limits are requests, input tokens and output tokens per minute, enforced as a token bucket, so a burst can fail even when the minute total looks fine. Do the arithmetic: 800 requests a minute at 4,000 input tokens each is 3.2 million input tokens per minute, which a 2 million limit will not allow. For most models cached input does not count toward the input limit, so caching a shared prefix is also a throughput fix. Spend limits are separate: a limit you set returns 400, the tier cap returns 429 with no retry-after, and retrying cures neither.

Reliable calls start by sorting errors by whether a retry can help. Transient errors, namely 429 with a retry-after header, 529 overloaded, 5xx, timeouts and dropped connections, are retried with exponential backoff and jitter, capped in attempts and wait, honoring retry-after. The SDK already retries twice by default, so do not stack your own loop on top without deciding which layer owns retries. Errors like 400, 401, 403, 404 and 413 will fail again until you change the request or credential. Make operations that charge or send idempotent, bound concurrency with a semaphore so asynchronous fan-out does not cause a wall of 429s, and add a circuit breaker and a fallback so a bad hour does not take the product down.

A Claude application is never finished. The life cycle loops through requirements, design, build, test, deploy, operate, maintain and retire. Test with evals gated in the CI pipeline. Deploy gradually behind a feature flag so you can roll back. Operate with monitoring that scores sampled live output and logs the prompt and model version per request. Maintain by tracking the model lifecycle of active, legacy, deprecated and retired, with at least 60 days' notice before a public model retires, and migrate by running your own evals on the replacement. Pinned IDs and versioned prompts are what make a rollback possible.

Ordinary habits still apply. Keep prompts, schemas and settings in version control and change them through reviewed pull requests. Review model-generated diffs as carefully as human ones, because passing tests prove only what the tests cover. Refactor in small tested steps, and migrate a large system incrementally behind an interface, the strangler pattern, instead of rewriting it. In CI, run Claude Code non-interactively with claude -p, preferably in bare mode, with the key coming from the pipeline's secret store.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to systems engineering? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Running a Claude application is like running a food truck. Requirements are the menu and the promises you make: what you serve (functional) and how fast, how cheaply and under which health rules (non-functional). Capacity limits are the size of the kitchen window; a lunch rush can overflow it even if the daily total is fine, so you queue orders instead of shouting them all at once. When the supplier is out of an ingredient (a 529), you wait and try again, but if your licence has expired (a 401) waiting will not help. Over the years the supplier retires products, so you keep a tested replacement and change the menu gradually.
commonTraps: Retrying every error. A 400, 401, 403 or a spend-cap 429 needs a code, credential or limit change, not another attempt.
Stacking a custom retry loop on top of the SDK's default retries and multiplying traffic during an incident.
Putting a latency-sensitive feature on the batch endpoint, or an overnight job on full-price synchronous calls.
Waiting for a model's retirement date before testing a replacement; deprecation notices exist to give you time to run evals.
Treating green tests as proof that a model-generated change is safe to merge without human review.
lessons.scenario: A telecom builds a support assistant and a nightly churn-analysis job. The team converts "fast and accurate" into a p95 first-token time of three seconds, an accuracy threshold on a labeled set and a cost per conversation. Chat streams synchronously; the analysis runs as batches at half price. At launch day 429s appear: the arithmetic shows input tokens per minute, not requests, are the binding limit, so a shared policy block is cached. The client retries only transient errors with capped backoff, evals gate every prompt change in CI, and a new model is rolled out to five percent of traffic behind a flag before everyone.
lessons.onTheJob: Write the non-functional requirements down before choosing a model, and do the token arithmetic against your real limits at peak, not average. Keep one place in the codebase that owns retries, timeouts and logging. Put an alert on spend before the tier cap, and another on the share of responses that end in max_tokens or refusal, since those quietly degrade quality. Put the model deprecation page on the team calendar, export the usage by model to find stragglers, and rehearse a rollback before you need one.

cheatSheet.heading: Agents and workflows: architecture (Domain 1)
points: Workflow: your code decides the path. Agent: the model decides the path. Use the least autonomy that meets the requirement; known, repeatable, auditable steps mean a workflow.

Workflow patterns: prompt chaining (fixed sequence with gates), routing (classify, then dispatch), parallelization (sectioning or voting, pieces known in advance), orchestrator-workers (pieces decided at run time), evaluator-optimizer (generate and critique with a round cap).
Use an agent when the path is unpredictable and each step depends on tool results. Always add turn and budget limits and a clear definition of done.
Subagent: fresh context window, restricted tools, only its final message returns. Benefits: context isolation, parallelism, specialised prompts. Costs: latency and tokens.
Subagents do NOT inherit the lead's conversation. The task prompt must carry file paths, error text, constraints and decisions made so far.
Manager/supervisor hierarchy: a lead delegates to specialists and merges reports. Justify each layer with different tools, permissions or context; deeper is not better.

Frameworks: LangGraph (graph of deterministic and model steps, durable state, human-in-the-loop), PydanticAI (typed tools, validated outputs), Strands Agents (open-source toolkit for production agents). They add abstraction; the tool_use contract underneath is unchanged.

cheatSheet.heading: Building agents: loop, SDK, Managed Agents, hooks (Domain 1)
points: Client-tool loop: send tools, stop_reason tool_use, run every tool, reply with ONE user message holding a tool_result per tool_use ID (results first), repeat until a reply has no tool request.

The model never executes client tools (custom, bash, text editor, memory, computer). Server tools (web_search, web_fetch, code_execution, tool_search) run on Anthropic infrastructure; pause_turn means send the assistant content back to continue.

Who owns the harness: custom loop on the Messages API (full control; SDK tool runner automates the simple case), Claude Agent SDK (Claude Code's loop as a Python/TypeScript library in your process), Claude Managed Agents (Anthropic-hosted harness).

Managed Agents (beta): agent + environment + session + events. Environment is an Anthropic-managed cloud sandbox or a self-hosted sandbox (execution and files stay with you; tool inputs and results still reach Anthropic). Best for long-running, asynchronous work; not eligible for zero data retention.

Agent SDK limits: max_turns (tool-use turns) and max_budget_usd (includes subagents; may overshoot by one response). ResultMessage subtype: success, error_max_turns, error_max_budget_usd, error_during_execution; result text exists only on success. Resume with the session ID.
Permission modes: default, acceptEdits, plan, dontAsk, auto, bypassPermissions (isolated environments only). allowed_tools auto-approves; disallowed_tools always blocks.

Hooks run in your process, not in context: PreToolUse (allow, modify or deny), PostToolUse, UserPromptSubmit, Stop, SubagentStart/Stop, PreCompact. Programmatic enforcement beats prompts and CLAUDE.md when consequences are severe.
Long runs: compaction can drop early instructions, so keep persistent rules in the system prompt or CLAUDE.md; use a memory store for cross-session facts; send noisy work to subagents.

cheatSheet.heading: Messages API essentials (Domain 2)
points: POST /v1/messages with x-api-key (or bearer token), anthropic-version: 2023-06-01 and JSON content type. Required body: model, max_tokens, messages. system is a top-level field. SDKs add the headers.
The API is stateless: resend the full history every call. A response's content is an array of blocks (text, tool_use, thinking...): loop and branch on type.

stop_reason values: end_turn, max_tokens (cut off), stop_sequence, tool_use, pause_turn, refusal (a normal HTTP 200, check stop_details), model_context_window_exceeded. Truncation and refusal are successful responses, not exceptions.

Streaming = server-sent events: message_start, content_block_start/delta/stop, message_delta (stop_reason and cumulative usage), message_stop; ping events; an error event can follow a 200. input_json_delta fragments are valid JSON only after the block stops.
Stream large outputs: SDKs reject non-streaming requests expected to exceed about ten minutes; default timeout is 10 minutes. Use the final-message helper when you do not need events.

Structured outputs: output_config.format with a JSON Schema guarantees shape, not truth. Exceptions: refusal and max_tokens. Schema limits: additionalProperties false, no recursion, no numeric or length constraints, minItems 0 or 1, not with citations.
Assistant prefill returns a 400 on Claude 4.6 and later. Thinking blocks (with signatures) must be passed back unchanged; thinking tokens are billed as output and count toward max_tokens.
Vision and PDF: image and document blocks from base64, URL or Files API file ID; images are JPEG, PNG, GIF or WebP; request cap 32 MB. count_tokens gives an estimate before sending.

cheatSheet.heading: Errors, limits, batch, files and platforms (Domain 2)
points: Status codes: 400 invalid_request, 401 authentication, 402 billing, 403 permission, 404 not_found, 413 request_too_large (32 MB Messages, 256 MB Batches, 500 MB Files), 429 rate_limit, 500 api_error, 504 timeout, 529 overloaded.

Retry with capped exponential backoff and jitter: 429 (honor retry-after), 5xx, 529, timeouts, dropped connections. Do not retry 400, 401, 403, 404 or 413. SDKs retry twice by default (max_retries): do not stack another loop blindly.

Limits are RPM, ITPM and OTPM per model, enforced as a token bucket (bursts can fail). Cache reads do not count toward ITPM for most models; max_tokens is not used for OTPM. Ramp traffic gradually to avoid acceleration limits.
Spend: a limit you set returns 400; the tier cap returns 429 with no retry-after (enforced_spend_limit_reached). Retrying fixes neither.

Message Batches API: 50% of standard price, up to 100,000 requests or 256 MB, usually under an hour and at most 24 hours, results kept 29 days. Unique custom_id (1-64 characters); results arrive in any order; outcomes succeeded, errored, canceled, expired (the last three unbilled); no streaming; validation happens after submission, so dry-run first.

Files API: upload once, reference by file_id; up to 500 MB per file; workspace-wide visibility, so never accept file IDs from end users; uploaded files cannot be downloaded; operations are free and content is billed as input. Word and Excel files must be converted to text or PDF.
Zero data retention: standard Messages calls and inline PDFs are eligible; the Files API, Batches and Managed Agents are not.

Platforms: direct Claude API (newest features first), Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud, Microsoft Foundry, Claude Platform on AWS. Features, limits and model IDs differ; Bedrock and Google Cloud take base64 sources only; on Google Cloud the model is in the URL and anthropic_version (vertex-2023-10-16) is in the body.
inference_geo (global or us) works on Claude 4.6 and later on the direct API. Log the request ID (request-id header, request_id in errors) for support.

cheatSheet.heading: Application design, configuration and life cycle (Domain 2)
points: Requirements: functional = what the system does; non-functional = how well (latency, throughput, availability, cost, residency, compliance). Turn vague words into measurable targets before choosing a design.
Realtime versus batch: a person waiting needs a streamed synchronous call; bulk, latency-tolerant work goes to batch. Do the token arithmetic against RPM, ITPM and OTPM, and cache shared prefixes.
Interfaces: claude.ai and the mobile apps add Anthropic's system prompt; the API sends only what you supply; Claude Code adds its own instructions plus your CLAUDE.md files.

Content boundary: instructions in the system prompt, untrusted material in delimited, labelled blocks or tool_result. Schema design: clear names and descriptions, enums for closed sets, required fields, shallow nesting, additionalProperties false; strict-schema limits are 20 strict tools, 24 optional parameters, 16 union-typed parameters.
Session hygiene (Claude Code): clear between unrelated tasks; after repeated failed corrections, clear and restart with a better prompt; delegate research to subagents; compact with instructions.

CLAUDE.md: managed, user, project (./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md), local (CLAUDE.local.md, git-ignored). Files are concatenated, not overridden; aim for under 200 lines; it is guidance, not enforcement; use .claude/rules for path-specific rules.

settings.json precedence, highest first: managed, command line, .claude/settings.local.json, .claude/settings.json, ~/.claude/settings.json. List keys such as permission allow rules merge across scopes.

Plugins bundle skills, subagents, hooks and MCP servers. Scopes: user, project (committed settings; each teammate still installs it), local. Enabled plugins put descriptions in context every turn; dependencies take semver ranges (~2.1.0); review before installing.

Pin the full model ID (dateless IDs from the 4.6 generation are fixed snapshots; aliases move). Version prompts in source control and log the version. Gate changes with evals in CI, roll out behind a flag, keep a rollback. Model lifecycle: active, legacy, deprecated, retired, with at least 60 days' notice.

cheatSheet.heading: Exam-day strategy
points: Format: 53 items, 120 minutes (about two minutes each), multiple-choice and multiple-response; every item states how many answers to select. Scoring is scaled 100 to 1,000 with a pass at 720, judged on the total. The report adds percent correct by domain, which does not decide pass or fail. Fee 125 USD; the credential is valid 12 months.

Weighting: Applications and Integration is 33.1% (roughly 17 to 18 items) and Agents and Workflows 14.7% (roughly 8 items), so roughly half the exam comes from this course. Model selection (16.8%), prompt and context engineering (11.0%) and tools and MCPs (10.6%) follow.

Questions are scenarios with a stem such as "Which approach BEST fits" or "What is the MOST appropriate". Read the final sentence first, then underline the constraint words: non-urgent, must never, severe consequences, reusable, real-time, zero data retention.

Name the principle before reading the options: least autonomy that works; enforce in code when it must always hold; batch for latency-tolerant bulk work; give subagents explicit context; separate untrusted input from instructions; match the fix to the failing layer.

Typical wrong options: prompt wording where a guarantee is needed, treating a symptom (higher temperature, bigger model, bigger limit), over-engineering (a multi-agent hierarchy for a simple task), skipping evals or review, and features that no longer exist (prefill on 4.6 and later).
Multi-select: select exactly the number requested. Judge each option against the scenario, not against whether it is true in general.
Pace: one quick pass answering what you know, flag the rest, then return with the remaining time. Leave about ten minutes at the end to review flagged items and confirm every item is answered.

Do not panic at unfamiliar product names; reason from the contract (stateless API, stop_reason, tool_use and tool_result, limits and retries). Use current names: Claude Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5.

madlibs.scenario: When the steps of a process are known in advance and must repeat identically on every run, the best design is a {b1}. When each next action depends on what the previous tool returned and the path cannot be predicted, the better fit is {b2}.

options: deep supervisor hierarchy
workflow with fixed code paths
fully autonomous agent
a fixed prompt chain
an agent loop with limits
a single routing step

madlibs.explanation: Known, repeatable, auditable steps point to a workflow, where code owns the order. Unpredictable, feedback-driven work is what an agent loop is for, ideally with turn and budget limits.

madlibs.scenario: A subagent starts with a fresh context, so the lead agent must put the file paths, error text and earlier decisions into the {b1}. When the subagent finishes, only its {b2} returns to the lead.

options: subagent's old tool results
task prompt it sends
lead agent's hidden system prompt
final message
entire working context window
complete transcript of every tool call

madlibs.explanation: The task prompt is the only channel from parent to subagent, and the subagent's intermediate reads and tool calls stay inside its own context, which is why delegation protects the lead's context window.

madlibs.scenario: To make sure an Agent SDK agent can never edit .env files, a {b1} hook that denies the call is the dependable choice, because a rule written in CLAUDE.md is only {b2}.

options: PostToolUse
PreToolUse
UserPromptSubmit
applied before every tool call
enforced configuration
context the model weighs

madlibs.explanation: A PreToolUse hook runs before the tool executes and can deny it in code. CLAUDE.md is loaded as context that the model usually follows but can miss, so it is guidance rather than enforcement. A PostToolUse hook would run only after the edit had happened.

madlibs.scenario: The Messages API is {b1}, so the application must resend the full history with every call. A response whose stop_reason is {b2} means the reply was cut off at the output cap and may be incomplete.

options: stateful
stateless
session-based
max_tokens
tool_use
end_turn

madlibs.explanation: The server keeps no conversation memory between calls. A stop_reason of max_tokens signals truncation; end_turn is a natural finish and tool_use is a request to run a tool.

madlibs.scenario: A 429 response that carries a {b1} header should be retried after that many seconds. A 429 caused by reaching the monthly {b2} has no such header and is not fixed by retrying.

options: anthropic-version
request-id
retry-after
request timeout
spend cap
burst allowance

madlibs.explanation: The retry-after header tells you how long to wait. The tier spend-cap variant returns the same status without that header and persists until access resumes or the limit is raised, so retries cannot help.

madlibs.scenario: Claude Code treats CLAUDE.md as {b1}, not enforced configuration, so a mandatory policy belongs in {b2} settings. For stable production behavior, pin the {b3} model ID instead of an alias that follows the newest release.

options: context
a hard rule
a sandbox
user
managed
local
wildcard
abbreviated
full

madlibs.explanation: CLAUDE.md is loaded as context the model weighs. Managed settings sit at the top of the precedence order, so users cannot override them. Aliases move with new releases, whereas a full model ID names a fixed version you can test and roll back to.

sequences.prompt: Put the steps of one pass through a client-side tool-use loop on the Messages API in order.
steps: Send the user message together with the tools array
Receive a reply with stop_reason tool_use and one or more tool_use blocks
Run each requested tool in your own code
Append the assistant reply, then one user message holding a tool_result for every tool_use ID, results first
Call the model again with the extended history
Stop looping when a reply arrives with no tool request
sequences.explanation: The model only requests tools; your code runs them and reports back. Every ID must be answered in a single user message with the results ahead of any text, and the loop ends on any stop reason other than tool_use, which you then handle on its own terms.

sequences.prompt: Put the main events of a streamed Messages API response in the order they arrive.
steps: message_start
content_block_start
content_block_delta (repeated)
content_block_stop
message_delta with the stop reason and cumulative usage
message_stop
sequences.explanation: A stream opens with the message shell, then each content block is bracketed by start and stop around its deltas. The message_delta near the end carries the stop_reason, because it is null in the first event, and message_stop closes the stream. Ping events can appear anywhere.

sequences.prompt: Order the steps for running a bulk job on the Message Batches API.
steps: Dry-run one request of each shape on the Messages API
Build the requests, each with a unique custom_id
Create the batch
Poll the processing status until it reads ended
Stream the results and match each one to its input by custom_id
Fix and resubmit the errored and expired requests in a new batch
sequences.explanation: Validate the request shape first because batch validation happens after submission. Results arrive in any order, so custom_id is the join key, and failed or expired items are repaired and resubmitted separately while the successes are kept.

sequences.prompt: Order the steps of a safe migration to a newer Claude model after a deprecation notice.
steps: Read the notice and note the retirement date and the recommended replacement
Run your own eval suite against the replacement model
Adjust prompts and parameters that behave differently
Send a small share of traffic to the new model behind a feature flag
Compare quality, latency and cost, then ramp up with a rollback path ready
Move all traffic and remove the old model ID before the retirement date
sequences.explanation: Use the notice period to test on your own tasks first, then expose real traffic gradually so a regression affects few users and can be reversed. Pinning the new ID and removing the old one completes the move before requests to the retired model would fail.

sequences.prompt: Put the steps of delegating a task to a subagent in order.
steps: The lead agent identifies a focused subtask that can be handled on its own
The lead writes a task prompt containing file paths, error text and constraints
The subagent starts in a fresh context with its own instructions and restricted tools
The subagent works through its tool calls without adding them to the lead's context
The subagent returns only its final message
The lead reads the report and merges it into its answer
sequences.explanation: The task prompt is the only thing handed over, so it is written before the subagent starts. The subagent's intermediate work stays in its own context window and only the closing message comes back for the lead to combine.

caseStudies.title: Northwind Mutual: A Claims Assistant Under Strict Data Rules
caseStudies.scenario: Northwind Mutual is building a claims assistant on the direct Claude API with a Claude 4.6-generation or later model. Adjusters upload scanned claim packets of 20 to 80 pages as PDFs and chat with the assistant, which must begin answering within a few seconds and also returns a structured record of claimant, dates and amounts. Every night the company re-extracts records from 120,000 archived claims after a taxonomy change, and the results are loaded into a warehouse the next morning. Compliance has two hard rules: inference must run only on US infrastructure, and Northwind's contract is a zero data retention arrangement. During the pilot an engineer uploaded packets through the Files API so the chat could reference them by ID. Three problems appeared: extractions on very long packets sometimes fail JSON parsing with replies that stop abruptly, calls return 429 at peak even though the request rate is well under the limit, and every request repeats the same 3,000-token instruction and policy block.

questions.question: Which design for handling the uploaded packets BEST fits the compliance rules?
options: Upload the PDFs to the Files API but set a short expiry, which restores zero data retention
Send the PDFs as base64 and rely on a system prompt telling Claude to use only US servers
Send each PDF inline as a document block in standard Messages calls, with inference_geo set to us
Keep the Files API uploads and reference the IDs, since uploads are deleted when each chat ends
